title: Teens Chase 200 Birds in 24 Hours at the World Series of Birding!
summary: Imagine running through a dark park at midnight, hoping to see a bird's tail poking out of a giant nest. That's how three teenage boys started their big adventure last weekend. Otys Train, 16, Jack Trojan, 17, and Zade Pacetti, 16, were competing in the 43rd World Series of Birding. The goal? Count as many bird species as possible in New Jersey in just 24 hours. They call themselves the Pete Dunnelins, a name mixing a shorebird called a dunlin and a famous birder, Pete Dunne. The competition began at midnight on Saturday. The boys jumped out of their SUV, ran across a field, and peered at nests on a pole. After 10 minutes, Otys shouted, "I got the monk parakeet!" It was their first bird of the day. They've been friends since 2021 and have won the high school division for the past two years. Last year, they tied for first with 199 species. This year, they want 200. They even made a spreadsheet planning every minute. But birds don't follow schedules. "You can't really predict when you're going to see or hear everything," Jack said. Their dads drove the van and made sure the boys ate and drank water, not just energy drinks and M&Ms. The team wore matching gray sweatshirts. In the dark, they listened carefully for marsh birds. Otys has memorized hundreds of bird calls. He can identify a sora's whinny or an American woodcock's "peent" instantly. The boys whispered and agreed on each bird before adding it to their list. It's a fun, exciting race against the clock—and nature.
why_it_matters: This shows how a hobby like birdwatching can turn into a thrilling challenge with friends, and you can explore nature even in the middle of the night.

background_read: The World Series of Birding is an annual event held in New Jersey since 1984. Teams race to spot the most bird species in a single day.
Birdwatching, or birding, is a popular hobby all over the world — some people even memorize hundreds of bird calls to identify them by sound.
Pete Dunne (a well-known bird expert and author) helped make birding famous, and the team named themselves after him and the dunlin bird.
